items.stem: Poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are made by addition polymerisation. Why are alkenes, rather than alkanes, used as the monomers?

options.text: Alkenes contain a C=C bond that can open to make new bonds
Alkanes are saturated, so their molecules join end to end
Alkene molecules are held by weak intermolecular forces
Ethane is used, since poly(ethene) is named after it

items.why: The specification states that alkenes are used to make addition polymers; the C=C is the group that opens so each monomer can bond to two neighbours.

items.stem: Which monomer is used to make poly(propene)?

options.text: Propane, because the polymer chain is completely saturated
Propene, because its molecules contain a C=C double bond
Ethene, because n is a small number like three
Propanol, because poly(propene) is named from –OH

items.why: Poly(propene) is the addition polymer of propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, named after the alkene monomer used.

items.stem: What happens to the molecules in an addition polymerisation reaction?

options.text: Monomers join and some atoms are lost
Many monomers join and water molecules are given off
Many small monomers join into one large molecule
Each chain grows to the same fixed length

items.why: The specification says many small molecules (monomers) join together to form very large molecules (polymers).

items.stem: Which statement about a sample of poly(ethene) is correct?

options.text: Every chain holds the same number of units
The units in a chain are held by weak forces
Each chain contains two joined ethene molecules
The chains are of many different lengths

items.why: n is not a fixed number: a sample contains chains built from different numbers of repeating units.

items.stem: The specification gives the example n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–n . What does this equation tell you?

options.text: n ethene molecules give one chain of n repeating units
n ethene molecules give a polymer and n waters
Two ethene molecules give a chain two units long
n ethene molecules give a chain that still has C=C

items.why: The same symbol n appears on both sides: every monomer molecule that reacts becomes one repeating unit in the chain.

items.stem: The repeating unit of poly(ethene) is –CH₂–CH₂–. Why does it contain the same atoms as the ethene monomer?

options.text: Because the water that is lost is later taken back in
Because no other molecule is formed in this reaction
Because two hydrogen atoms are lost from each end
Because the C=C double bond is kept in the chain

items.why: This is the reason the specification gives: nothing else is produced, so every atom of the monomer stays in the repeating unit.

items.stem: 500 g of ethene is completely polymerised. Which statement about the atoms involved is correct?

options.text: Some atoms leave because a small molecule is released
The polymer holds more carbon atoms per hydrogen
All the atoms end up in the poly(ethene) formed
One hydrogen per monomer ends off the chain

items.why: No other molecule is formed, so every atom from the ethene is in the polymer and 500 g of poly(ethene) is produced.

items.stem: Which feature of a molecule shows that it can be a monomer for addition polymerisation?

options.text: An –OH group on an end carbon
A fully saturated carbon chain
A C=C double bond at either end
A carbon–carbon double bond

items.why: The specification asks students to recognise monomers from the presence of the functional group C=C.

items.stem: Which description is of an addition polymer rather than of a monomer?

options.text: A repeating unit in brackets with no bonds crossing them
A short molecule that holds just one C=C double bond
A repeating unit in brackets with bonds through them and n
A long molecule with an –OH group at each of its ends

items.why: The specification's form for a polymer is the repeating unit in brackets, with extension bonds through the brackets and n outside.

items.stem: Chloroethene is CH₂=CHCl. Which description of the equation for its polymerisation is correct?

options.text: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets plus n HCl given off
n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets keeping the C=C
Two CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets with a 2 shown
n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets with n on the right

items.why: n monomer molecules give a chain of n repeating units, –(CH₂–CHCl)–n, with no other product.

items.stem: When the repeating unit of an addition polymer is drawn, why are bonds drawn through the brackets?

options.text: To show more units are joined on both sides of it
To show the unit is a complete and separate molecule
To show where the double bond once was in the monomer
To show the point at which each chain stops

items.why: The extension bonds show that the unit is one link in a long chain, not a separate molecule.

items.stem: The repeating unit of a polymer is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. Which molecule was the monomer?

options.text: Propane, as all bonds are single
Propene, since the C=C re-forms
Butene, as the unit has 4 carbons
Propanol, since a small molecule leaves

items.why: The repeating unit has three carbons; putting the double bond back between the two chain carbons gives propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.

items.stem: Tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂, undergoes addition polymerisation. What is the repeating unit of the polymer?

options.text: –CF₂=CF₂– with the double bond still in place
–CF₂–CF₂– without bonds through the brackets
–CF₂–CF₂– with the bonds drawn through the brackets
–CF₂–CF₂– after two fluorine atoms are lost

items.why: The C=C opens to a single bond, the atoms are unchanged, and extension bonds show the unit joining on both sides.

items.stem: What must a monomer have in order to take part in condensation polymerisation?

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond in each of the monomers
One functional group at one end of a chain
A boiling point low enough for it to condense
Two functional groups in each monomer molecule

items.why: The specification states that condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups.

items.stem: Why is this type of polymerisation called condensation polymerisation?

options.text: A small molecule such as water is lost each time
A gas condenses to a liquid as the polymer is made
Steam given off turns back into liquid water
Carbon dioxide gas is given off as chains grow

items.why: The specification says the monomers join together, usually losing small molecules such as water, and so the reactions are called condensation reactions.

items.stem: The simplest condensation polymers are made from two different monomers. What is true of those two monomers?

options.text: Each carries two different groups
Each has two of the same group
Each carries one group at an end
Each carries a C=C and an –OH group

items.why: The specification states that the simplest polymers come from two different monomers with two of the same functional groups on each monomer.

items.stem: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid are heated together. Which statement describes the polymerisation?

options.text: Many ethanediol molecules join each other, losing water
The two monomers join with no other product formed
The two different monomers join alternately, losing water
The two monomers join and carbon dioxide is given off

items.why: An ester link needs an –OH group and a –COOH group, so the diol and the diacid alternate, releasing water at each link.

items.stem: Which description of the monomer ethanediol is correct?

options.text: Two carbon atoms, with a single –OH group on it
Two carbon atoms, with a –COOH at each end
Two carbons joined by a C=C double bond
Two carbon atoms, with an –OH group on each

items.why: Ethanediol is HOCH₂CH₂OH: 'eth' gives two carbons and 'diol' gives two –OH groups.

items.stem: Hexanedioic acid is the second monomer used to make this polyester. Which description of it is correct?

options.text: Six carbon atoms, with a –COOH group at each end
Six carbon atoms, with just one –COOH group on an end
Six carbon atoms, with an –OH group at either end
Six carbon atoms, with a –COOH and an –NH₂ end

items.why: Hexanedioic acid is HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH: 'hexane' gives six carbons and 'dioic acid' gives two –COOH groups.

items.stem: What is produced when ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise together?

options.text: A polyester and no other product
A polyester and water molecules
A polypeptide and water molecules
A polyester and carbon dioxide gas

items.why: The –OH and –COOH groups react to form ester links along the chain, releasing a molecule of water at each link.

items.stem: Amino acids can polymerise on their own, without a second kind of monomer. Why is this possible?

options.text: Each molecule has two of the same functional group
Each molecule has a carbon–carbon double bond
Each molecule carries two different functional groups
Each molecule carries one group that reacts twice

items.why: The specification states that amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule, an –NH₂ and a –COOH, so one monomer can link at both ends.

items.stem: Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH. Which groups react when glycine molecules polymerise, and what is lost?

options.text: –NH₂ with –COOH, losing one ammonia molecule
Two –COOH groups, losing a water molecule
C=C with –COOH, losing a water molecule
–NH₂ with –COOH, losing one water molecule

items.why: The two different groups on neighbouring molecules react together, and H from –NH₂ with OH from –COOH leaves as water.

items.stem: How does a protein differ from a polypeptide made from a single kind of amino acid?

options.text: Different amino acids are combined in one chain
The same amino acid is repeated along the whole chain
Two separate chains are twisted round each other
Whole polypeptides act as the monomers used

items.why: The specification states that different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins.

items.stem: Why is DNA described as essential for life?

options.text: It forms the plastic parts of cells
It encodes genetic instructions
It supplies the amino acids needed
It is a protein that speeds reactions

items.why: The specification states that DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

items.stem: Which statement describes the structure of most DNA molecules?

options.text: One polymer chain coiled into a double helix
Four polymer chains, one per type of nucleotide
Two polymer chains in the form of a double helix
Two chains, each built from two nucleotides

items.why: The specification states that most DNA molecules are two polymer chains in the form of a double helix.

items.stem: Which list contains only naturally occurring polymers?

options.text: DNA, proteins, starch and poly(ethene)
DNA, glucose, starch and cellulose
DNA, proteins, glucose and starch
DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose

items.why: These are the naturally occurring polymers important for life that the specification names.

items.stem: Name the type of monomer from which both starch and cellulose are made.

options.text: Glucose molecules build both these polymers
Amino acids build both of these long polymers
Starch molecules join together to make cellulose
Nucleotides build both of these polymers

items.why: Starch and cellulose are both naturally occurring polymers of glucose.

items.stem: Which statement correctly matches these naturally occurring polymers to their monomers?

options.text: Proteins from nucleotides; DNA from the amino acids
Proteins from amino acids; DNA from nucleotides
Proteins from amino acids; DNA from glucose units
Proteins from glucose; DNA from the four nucleotides

items.why: Proteins are polymers of amino acids and DNA is built from four different nucleotides.

items.stem: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise. What is shown in the repeating unit of the polymer formed?

options.text: An ester link, with bonds drawn through the brackets
An ester link, with the brackets closed off
A peptide link joining the two monomer units
Two ethanediol units joined to one another

items.why: An –OH group and a –COOH group react to give an ester link, and the extension bonds show the unit repeating along the chain.

items.stem: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, polymerises to make a polypeptide. What is the repeating unit of that polypeptide?

options.text: –NH₂–CH₂–COOH– with bonds through the brackets
–NH–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets
–O–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets
–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets

items.why: The H lost from –NH₂ and the OH lost from –COOH leave as water, so –NH–CH₂–CO– repeats along the chain.
